title: Kiwanuka v Attorney General of the Republic of Uganda (Reference No. 29 of 2020)  (First Instance Division)
text:
REFERENCE NO. 29 OF 2020
MALE H. MABIRIZI K. KIWANUKA ................................... APPLICANT
VERSUS
THE ATTORNEY GENERAL OF
THE REPUBLIC OF UGANDA ............................. RESPONDENT
31 MARCH 2026
ST

JUDGMENT OF THE COURT
A. INTRODUCTION
1. This Reference was filed on 8th September 2020 by Mr Male H.
Mabirizi K. Kiwanuka ("the Applicant"), a Ugandan citizen and
resident, against the Attorney General of the Republic of Uganda
("the Respondent").
2. It challenges the Presidential nomination, Parliamentary approval,
subsequent appointment and swearing-in of Hon. Justice Alphonse
Chigamoy Owiny-Dollo as Chief Justice and Hon. Justice Richard
Buteera as Deputy Chief Justice of the Republic of Uganda.
3. The Reference is brought under Articles 23(1 ), 27(1) and 30(1) of
the Treaty for the Establishment of the East African Community ("the
Treaty") and Rule 25(1) of the East African Court of Justice Rules of
the Court, 2019 ("the Rules").
B. PARTIES
4. The Applicant, Mr. MALE H. Mabirizi K. Kiwanuka, is a natural
person, a citizen and resident of the Republic of Uganda, a Partner
State of the East African Community. His address of service for the
purposes of this Reference is c/o Plot 35, Kampala Road, Post
Office Building, 5th Floor, Room 501A, Kampala, Uganda.
5. The Respondent is the Attorney General of the Republic of Uganda,
sued in his official capacity as the Principal Legal Advisor of the
Government of the Republic of Uganda. His address of service is:
the Republic of Uganda, Ministry of Justice and Constitutional
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 2

Affairs, Directorate of Civil Litigation, Bowman House, Parliament
Avenue, Kampala.
C. REPRESENTATION
th
5. At the hearing on 13 November 2025, the Applicant appeared in
person.
6. The Respondent was represented by Mr Wanyama Kodoli, Assistant
Commissioner, Ms Apita Susan Akello, Senior State Attorney, and
Ms Amucu Daniella, State Attorney.
D. THE APPLICANT'S CASE
7. The Applicant's case is comprehensively set out in the Statement of
th
Reference filed on 8 September 2020, the supporting Affidavit
th
affirmed on 7 September 2020 (together with annextures "A" and
"B" being his two petitions/caveats dated 2pt August 2020), the
Reply to the Respondent's Response, and his written submissions
highlighted at the hearing.
8. The gravamen of the Reference is that the entire process adopted
in the Presidential nomination, Parliamentary approval, appointment
and swearing-in of Hon. Justice Alphonse Chigamoy Owiny-Dollo
as Chief Justice and Hon. Justice Richard Buteera as Deputy Chief
Justice was unlawful and infringed Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the
Treaty. The Applicant particularises seven specific defects in
respect of the Deputy Chief Justice appointment:
a) Hon. Justice Richard Buteera was nominated to a
position that was not vacant at the material time, it
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 3

being still occupied by Hon. Justice Alphonse
Chigamoy Owiny-Dollo;
b) The Judicial Service Commission never declared the
Deputy Chief Justice position vacant, never advertised
it, never conducted interviews, and never selected
candidates for it;
c) Hon. Justice Richard Buteera never applied for the
position of Deputy Chief Justice (he had applied only
for Chief Justice);
d) The Judicial Service Commission never advised the
President to appoint Hon. Justice Richard Buteera as
Deputy Chief Justice;
e) Parliament failed to address the Applicant's two
petitions/caveats against the approval of both
nominees, never reverted to him, and never invited him
for interaction;
f) The Parliamentary vetting by the Appointments
Committee was conducted in camera, closed to the
public and the press; and
g) The Report of the Appointments Committee was never
presented to the Parliamentary plenary for debate and
voting.
9. The Applicant relies on Article 142(1) of the Constitution of Uganda
1995 which requires appointment by the President acting on the
advice of the Judicial Service Commission (JSC) and with the
approval of Parliament and Article 147(1 )(a) regarding JSC
functions.
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 4

10. He further invokes the Parliamentary Rules of Procedure 2017, the
National Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy, and
various provisions of the Constitution guaranteeing participatory
democracy, accountability and the rule of law.
11. He argues that these procedural omissions and the alleged secrecy
amounted to a breach of the fundamental and operational principles
of the Community under Articles 6(d) which provides for good
governance including democracy, rule of law, accountability and
transparency and 7(2) of the Treaty.
12. The Applicant seeks the following:
(i) Declarations that:
a) the Republic of Uganda's actions decisions of
nomination, approval and appointment as well as the
process adopted in presidential nomination,
approval, subsequent appointment and swearing in
of Hon. Justice Alphonse Chigamoy Owiny-Dollo and
Hon. Justice Richard Buteera, as Chief Justice and
Deputy Chief of the Republic of Uganda,
respectively, are unlawful and infringements on the
fundamental and operational principles the
Community which include good governance
including adherence to the principles of democracy,
the rule of law, accountability, transparency and
maintenance of universally accepted standards of
human rights to the extent particularized in the
Reference;
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 5

b) Hon. Justice Richard Buteera was nominated to the
position of Deputy Chief Justice which was not
vacant at the time of nomination, approval and
appointment, it being occupied by Hon. Justice
Alfonse Chigamoy Owiny-Dollo;
c) The Uganda Judicial Service Commission has never
declared the position of Deputy Chief Justice vacant,
never advertised it, never conducted interviews and
never selected candidates for the same;
d) Hon. Justice Richard Buteera never applied to
become a Deputy Chief Justice;
e) The Uganda Judicial Service Commission has never
advised the President to appoint Hon. Justice
Richard Buteera as Deputy Chief Justice;
f) Parliament of Uganda failed to address the
Applicant's petition/caveat against the approval of
two persons and indeed neither reverted back to the
Applicant nor invited him for interaction; and
g) The parliamentary vetting of Honourable Justice
Alfonse Chigamoy Owiny-Dollo and Hon.Justice
Richard Buteera, as Chief Justice and Deputy Chief
Justice, duo was closed out to the public and the
press, and the report of parliamentary appointments
committee was never represented to the
parliamentary plenary for debate and voting.
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 6

(ii) Orders annulling:
a) The appointment and assumption of office of by
Hon.Justice Alfonse Chigamoy Owiny-Dollo as
Chief Justice of the Republic of Uganda;
b) The appointment and assumption of office of by
Hon.Justice Richard Buteera as Deputy Chief
Justice of the Republic of Uganda;
(iii) A permanent injunction restraining Uganda Government
from maintaining Hon.Justice Alfonse Chigamoy Owiny
Dollo and Hon. Justice Richard Buteera, as Chief Justice
and Deputy Chief justice of the Republic of Uganda;
(iv) General damages to the Applicant due to disturbance
and anguish caused to the Applicant arising out of the
actions, decisions and directives complained against in
this Reference;
(v) costs of the Reference to the Applicant; and
(vi) Interest of 6% per annum on general damages and costs
awarded to the Applicant from the time of filing this
Reference till payment in full.
E. THE RESPONDENT'S CASE
13. The Respondent denies each and every allegation of fact and law
contained in the Reference and puts the Applicant to the strictest
proof thereof.
14. The Respondent's defence is articulated in the Response to the
Reference filed on 23rd October 2020, the Affidavit of Jane L.
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 7

Kibirige, Clerk to Parliament, sworn on 23rd October 2022, the
Affidavit of Mwebembezi Julius, Registrar of the Judicial Service
Commission and the written submissions highlighted during the
hearing.
15. The Respondent firmly maintains that the nomination,
Parliamentary approval, appointment and swearing-in of both the
Chief Justice and the Deputy Chief Justice were lawful, transparent,
and in complete conformity with the Constitution of Uganda 1995
and the Treaty.
16. That the Judicial Service Commission duly declared the vacancy
for the office of Chief Justice, advertised it in accordance with
Regulation 16 of the Judicial Service Commission Regulations,
shortlisted three qualified candidates (including Hon. Justice Owiny
Dollo, then Deputy Chief Justice, and Hon. Justice Richard
Buteera), conducted interviews, graded and ranked the candidates
on merit, and formally advised the President on the appointment to
the office of Chief Justice.
17. That upon the successful appointment of Hon. Justice Owiny-Dollo
as Chief Justice, the office of Deputy Chief Justice became vacant
ipso facto by operation of law. The President, acting on the advice
already received from the Judicial Service Commission during the
Chief Justice recruitment process and in full exercise of his
constitutional powers under Articles 142(1) and 147(1)(a),
appointed Hon. Justice Richard Buteera, who had already been
rigorously vetted and favourably ranked in the same process, to the
newly vacant office of Deputy Chief Justice. That this was a logical,
consequential and cost-effective appointment that ensured
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 8

seamless continuity in the leadership of the Judiciary without the
need for a duplicative and wasteful recruitment exercise.
18. Regarding the Parliamentary approval process, the Respondent
avers that both nominations were properly considered and approved
by the Appointments Committee in strict accordance with the Rules
of Procedure of Parliament 2017. The proceedings of the
Appointments Committee were lawfully conducted in closed session
pursuant to Rule 162(2). The Chairperson duly reported to the
House in accordance with Rule 167, and the report was not subject
to debate as expressly provided by the Rules. That the Applicant's
petitions or caveats were received by the Clerk, tabled before the
Business Committee, and considered by the Appointments
Committee on their merits.
19. The Respondent emphasises that these procedures represent a
valid and constitutional delegation by Parliament under Articles 90
and 94 of the Constitution. That compliance with Parliament's own
Rules cannot, by any stretch of imagination, constitute secrecy or
procedural impropriety.
20. The Respondent places strong and decisive reliance on the
authoritative decision of the High Court of Uganda in Citizen Alert
Foundation (CAF) & Others vs Attorney General, Miscellaneous
Cause No. 339 of 2020. In that case, the identical challenge to the
nomination and appointment of Hon. Justice Richard Buteera as
Deputy Chief Justice was thoroughly litigated and dismissed. Justice
Ssekaana, after a full adversarial hearing, held unequivocally that
the process was "legal and procedurally proper".
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 9

21. The Respondent further notes that related constitutional and rule
of-law issues raised by the same Applicant have been adjudicated
upon by the Supreme Court of Uganda in Male H. Mabirizi
Kiwanuka & Others vs Attorney General, Consolidated
Constitutional Appeals Nos. 2, 3 & 4 of 2018.
22. The Respondent submits that respect for judicial and constitutional
independence is itself a fundamental expression of the rule of law,
as powerfully articulated by this Court in James Katabazi & 21
Others vs Secretary General of the EAC & Attorney General of
Uganda, EACJ Reference No. 1 of 2007.
23. On the question of burden of proof, the Respondent submits that it
is a trite and well-settled principle that he who alleges must prove.
That the Applicant has failed to adduce any credible, authentic or
reliable evidence capable of substantiating his serious claims of
breach of either the Constitution or the Treaty. The Respondent
relies on this Court's decisions in Henry Kyarimpa vs Attorney
General (supra) and East Africa Law Society vs Attorney
General of Kenya & Another, EACJ Reference No. 3 of 2010,
where it was held that the burden of proof in Treaty references lies
strictly on the Applicant and that mere allegations or technical
irregularities, however strongly asserted, are insufficient to establish
a breach.
24. The Respondent further cites East Africa Law Society vs
Attorney General & EAC Secretary General, EACJ Reference
No. 2 of 2011 for the principle that "it is not enough to allege a fact ...
the Applicant must bring forth credible, authentic, reliable and
admissible evidence to support such allegation".
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 10

25. In conclusion, the Respondent prays that the Reference be
dismissed with costs, as the Applicant's expansive and largely
unsubstantiated challenge has unnecessarily burdened public
resources and the judicial process of this Court.
F. ISSUES FOR DETERMINATION
26. The following issues were framed at the Scheduling Conference
held on 27th February 2025:
(i) Whether the Respondent's appointment of Hon. Justice
Alphonse Chigamoy Owiny-Dollo and Hon. Justice
Richard Buteera as Chief Justice and Deputy Chief
Justice respectively was unlawful and infringed Articles
G(d) and 7(2) of the Treaty; and
(ii)Whether the parties are entitled to the reliefs sought.
G. COURT'S DETERMINATION
ISSUE 1: Whether the Respondent's appointment of Hon.
Justice Alphonse Chigamoy Owiny-Dollo and Hon.
Justice Richard Buteera as Chief Justice and
Deputy Chief Justice respectively was unlawful and
infringed Articles G(d) and 7(2) of the Treaty.
27. The Applicant's challenge to the appointments is on two main
fronts.
(i) Parliamentary Approval Process
28. The Applicant alleges that the Parliamentary vetting was closed to
the public and press, that his petitions/caveats were ignored, and
the Appointments Committee report was never presented to the
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 11

plenary for debate and voting, which in his opinion was unlawful. He
relies on the South African Constitutional Court decision in Doctors
for Life International vs Speaker of the National Assembly &
Others (CCT 12/05) to brace his allegation.
29. We state upfront that this contention is misconceived.
30. Crucially, citizen participation in Uganda is constitutionally
guaranteed through representation, not through direct or
referendum-style involvement in every parliamentary process.
Article 38(1) of the Constitution of Uganda 1995 provides:
"Every Ugandan citizen has the right to participate in the
affairs of government, individually or through his or her
representatives in accordance with law."
31. The phrase "in accordance with law" is decisive. In Uganda's
representative democracy, citizens participate primarily through
their elected Members of Parliament. Parliament's Rules of
Procedure, duly made under Article 94, constitute the "law" that
governs how that representation is exercised. The Appointments
Committee acts as a specialised arm of the plenary, performing
delegated functions on behalf of the entire House. Its closed
proceedings and non-debatable report are therefore attributable to
Parliament as a whole and satisfy the constitutional requirement of
representation.
32. This system is fundamentally different from that considered in
Doctors for Life International vs Speaker of the National
Assembly & Others, In South Africa, the Constitution expressly
imposes an obligation on Parliament to "facilitate public
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 12

involvement" in legislative processes (Sections 59 and 72). The
Constitutional Court held that inadequate public hearings and
rushed timelines violated that specific constitutional duty, rendering
the legislative process defective. Uganda's Constitution contains no
equivalent mandatory public-hearing requirement for appointments
or committee work. Instead, it entrusts elected representatives with
the duty to act on behalf of the people, subject to the Rules of
Procedure. The Ugandan model is one of mediated representation,
not direct participatory law-making. Doctors for Life (supra) is
distinguishable.
33. This Court has previously addressed and upheld identical
parliamentary procedures. In Male H. Mabirizi K. Kiwanuka vs
Attorney General, EACJ Reference No. 8 of 2020, the Court
considered complaints of closed committee vetting and lack of
plenary debate during appointments. We held that such processes
are lawful delegations under Articles 90 and 94 of the Ugandan
Constitution and do not breach Articles 6(d) or 7(2) of the Treaty.
Public participation under Article 38 of the Constitution is
guaranteed "in accordance with law", the law here includes
Parliament's Rules.
34. The same position was taken in the Legal Brains Trust vs
Attorney General of Uganda, EACJ Reference No. 15 of 2020,
which also questioned parliamentary procedures on appointments.
35. In those cases, this Court emphasised that parliamentary
committees perform delegated functions on behalf of the whole
House, and that closed sessions for sensitive vetting are a
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 13

recognised and legitimate tool to ensure efficiency while maintaining
accountability through the final report to the House.
36. The approval process was therefore conducted in compliance with
the law. We find no violation.
(ii)The Judicial Service Commission (JSC) process and the
"consequential" appointment of the Deputy Chief Justice.
37. Turning to the core of the Applicant's challenge regarding the
Deputy Chief Justice appointment, the Court finds that the
appointment process was lawfully satisfied. The Judicial Service
Commission (JSC) discharged its constitutional duty under Article
142(1) when it advertised the Chief Justice vacancy, shortlisted
three eminently qualified candidates, including the then sitting
Deputy Chief Justice Owiny-Dollo and Justice Buteera, conducted
interviews, ranked the candidates on merit, and tendered formal
advice to the President on the Chief Justice appointment, per
Mwebembezi Julius affidavit and the Respondent's Response.
38. Upon the valid appointment and assumption of office by Justice
Owiny-Dollo as Chief Justice, the office of Deputy Chief Justice
became vacant ipso facto, automatically and by inevitable operation
of law.
39. The President then promptly filled that newly vacant office by
appointing Justice Buteera, who had already undergone thorough
vetting and ranking in the very same senior judicial recruitment
exercise. This consequential appointment was thereafter duly
approved by Parliament.
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 14

40. This integrated and logical process fully satisfied Article 142(1) of
the Constitution, which requires the President to act "on the advice
of the Judicial Service Commission", not a duplicative, separate
cycle for every consequential vacancy created by a lawful elevation.
41. The issue before us is not novel. Ugandan courts have repeatedly
considered and upheld precisely this type of judicial succession
process. In Citizen Alert Foundation (CAF) & Others vs Attorney
General (supra), the High Court directly adjudicated the identical
challenge to Justice Buteera's DCJ appointment. The applicants
raised the same grounds now advanced here: that the position was
allegedly not vacant at nomination; no separate JSC vacancy
declaration, advertisement, interviews or dedicated advice existed;
and that the process was therefore procedurally improper under
Article 142(1 ). The Court rejected these arguments in full, holding
that the JSC's advice in the Chief Justice process satisfied the
constitutional requirements for the consequential DCJ appointment.
The court emphasised separation of powers, institutional continuity,
and the limits of judicial review in high-level constitutional
appointments.
42. In Gerald Kafureeka Karuhanga vs Attorney General
(Constitutional Petition No. 39 of 2013), the court stressed the
tripartite nature of Article 142(1) appointments but made clear that
the President acts on JSC advice already given for the senior judicial
tier. The court warned against any interpretation that would allow
the executive to bypass the JSC entirely, but it did not prohibit logical
consequential appointments within an already-completed process,
precisely what occurred in the instant case.
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 15

43. Broader rule-of-law challenges to constitutional processes raised
by the same Applicant were also rejected by the Supreme Court in
Male H. Mabirizi Kiwanuka & Others vs Attorney General
(supra). The Supreme Court upheld the validity of parliamentary and
executive actions when they complied with the constitutional
framework, emphasising holistic interpretation over isolated
technical objections.
44. These authorities collectively establish beyond doubt that the
process followed for Justice Buteera's appointment was lawful
under Ugandan law.
45. This Court's own jurisprudence demands the same deference. In
Male Mabirizi vs Attorney General (supra), we upheld analogous
appointment processes entailing closed parliamentary vetting and
consequential appointments, despite complaints of procedural
irregularities and lack of public input. The Court emphasised that
Articles 6(d) and 7(2) do not override domestic constitutional
mechanisms when they are substantially followed.
46. Critically, this Court has repeatedly stressed the high standard of
proof required to establish a Treaty breach. In Henry Kyarimpa vs
Attorney General (supra), the Appellate Division made clear that
"the burden of proof in EACJ References lies strictly with the
Applicanf' and that mere allegations or technical irregularities are
insufficient.
47. A Partner State's action is not a Treaty violation unless it
demonstrates a clear, proven disregard of its own laws rising to the
level of undermining the rule of law. Simple procedural
disagreements, even if sincerely advanced, do not suffice.
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 16

48. This high threshold is rooted in the foundational principle articulated
in James Katabazi & 21 Others vs Secretary General of the EAC
& Attorney General of Uganda, EACJ Reference No. 1 of 2007,
where the Court stated that: "respect for judicial and constitutional
independence is itself an expression of the rule of law." The Treaty
protects constitutional independence by respecting Partner States'
domestic frameworks, not by second-guessing them on
technicalities.
49. The same strict burden was reiterated in East Africa Law Society
vs Attorney General of Kenya, EACJ Reference No. 3 of 2010.
The Court stated:
"It is not enough to allege a fact, however notorious one may
consider it to be... the Applicant must bring forth credible,
authentic, reliable and admissible evidence to support such
allegation."
50. The Applicant did not discharge the high standard of proof required
to establish any Treaty breach. In our opinion, technical
disagreement over the precise form of JSC documentation does not
constitute the systemic breach required to invoke Articles 6(d) and
7(2) of the Treaty.
51. The present Reference, to the extent it re-litigates the very issues
determined by the High Court in Citizen Alert Foundation (CAF}
(supra), and Male H. Mabirizi Kiwanuka & Others vs Attorney
General (supra), appears in substance to be a disguised appeal
from domestic decisions. This Court is not an appellate court over
domestic law rulings.
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 17

52. Absent evidence to the contrary, we find that the appointments
were made in full compliance with the Constitution of Uganda and,
in consequence, did not infringe Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the Treaty
53. Issue 1 is answered in the negative.
ISSUE 2: Whether The Parties are entitled to the reliefs sought
54. Having found no unlawfulness or Treaty infringement, the Applicant
is not entitled to any of the declarations, annulments, injunction,
damages or costs sought.
55. In any event, both Hon. Justice Alphonse Chigamoy Owiny-Dollo
and Hon. Justice Richard Buteera have since retired from office, the
former on 18 January 2026 upon attaining the mandatory retirement
age of 70 years, and the latter on 9 April 2025. The Reference is
therefore moot on the question of annulment or injunction.
56. The doctrine of mootness is firmly established in this Court's
jurisprudence. Courts do not decide academic or hypothetical
questions that no longer present a live controversy with practical
effect on the rights of the parties.
57. In Attorney General of Tanzania vs African Network for Animal
Welfare, EACJ Appeal No. 3 of 2014, this Court declined to grant
relief where the events complained of had been overtaken by time,
holding that judicial power is exercised to resolve actual disputes,
not to pronounce on abstract or spent issues.
58. Similarly, in Alcon International Ltd vs Standard Chartered
Bank of Uganda, EACJ Appeal No. 3 of 2013, the Court
emphasised that once the substratum of the dispute disappears, the
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 18

Court must refrain from embarking on an academic exercise that
serves no useful purpose.
59. This principle finds strong support in persuasive authority from
other jurisdictions.
60. In the leading Canadian Supreme Court decision Borowski vs
Attorney General of Canada [1989] 1 SCR 342, the Court
articulated a three-part test for mootness:
(i) whether a live controversy remains;
(ii) whether the decision would have a practical effect on
the rights of the parties; and
(iii) whether the Court should exercise its discretion to
hear the case notwithstanding mootness, considering
factors such as the public interest in resolution of an
important legal issue.
61. Applying that test here, no live controversy remains: the
appointments have long since ended with the retirement of both
office holders, and annulment or injunction would have no practical
effect.
62. While the Court retains a narrow discretion to hear moot matters of
exceptional public importance, that discretion is not engaged. The
public interest in clarifying judicial appointment processes has
already been amply served through the domestic proceedings in
Citizen Alert Foundation (supra) and Male H. Mabirizi Kiwanuka
& Others vs Attorney General (consolidated) (supra). There is
therefore no justification for this Court to pronounce on a now
academic question.
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 19

H. CONCLUSION
63. For all the foregoing reasons, the Court is satisfied that the
nomination, Parliamentary approval, appointment and swearing-in
of Hon. Justice Alphonse Chigamoy Owiny-Dollo as Chief Justice
and Hon. Justice Richard Buteera as Deputy Chief Justice were
carried out in strict compliance with the Constitution of the Republic
of Uganda and did not infringe the fundamental and operational
principles of the Treaty under Articles 6(d) and 7(2).
64. The process was neither shrouded in secrecy nor procedurally
flawed. On the contrary, it represented a lawful, transparent and
pragmatic exercise of constitutional authority that ensured continuity
in the leadership of the Judiciary.
65. The Applicant has failed to discharge the high evidentiary burden
required to establish any Treaty violation. Mere technical
disagreements over procedural steps, even when sincerely held, do
not rise to the level of a breach of the rule of law or good governance
as protected by the Treaty. This Court, while fully seized of its
jurisdiction under Article 30(1 ), must respect the constitutional
sovereignty of Partner States in matters of judicial appointments
unless a clear and proven infringement of the Treaty is
demonstrated, which has not been shown here.
66. In any event, both distinguished office holders have long since
retired from service. Any declaratory or annulment relief would now
be purely academic and of no practical utility.
67. Accordingly, the Reference is dismissed in its entirety.
Reference No. 29 of 2020 Page 20

68. However, having regard to the important public interest questions
raised concerning judicial appointments in a Partner State each
party shall bear its own costs.
69. It is so ordered
Dated, signed and delivered at Arusha this 31st Day of March,2026.
Hon. Justice Yohane B. Masara
